This article is part of the topic “Precision Cognitive Science: Developing Detailed Individual Models Within a Cognitive Architecture,” Andrea Stocco (Topic Editor).

# Personalized Model-Driven Interventions for Decisions From Experience

Edward A. Cranford,<sup>a</sup> Christian Lebiere,<sup>a</sup> Cleotilde Gonzalez,<sup>b</sup> Palvi Aggarwal,<sup>c</sup> Sterling Somers,<sup>a</sup> Konstantinos Mitsopoulos,<sup>d</sup> Milind Tambe<sup>e</sup>

<sup>a</sup>Department of Psychology, Carnegie Mellon University <sup>b</sup>Department of Social and Decision Sciences, Carnegie Mellon University <sup>c</sup>Department of Computer Science, The University of Texas at El Paso d School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University <sup>e</sup>Center for Research on Computation and Society, Harvard University

Received 29 June 2022; received in revised form 20 September 2024; accepted 27 September 2024

## Abstract

Cognitive models that represent individuals provide many benefits for understanding the full range of human behavior. One way in which individual differences emerge is through differences in knowledge. In dynamic situations, where decisions are made from experience, models built upon a theory of experiential choice (instance-based learning theory; IBLT) can provide accurate predictions of individual human learning and adaptivity to changing environments. Here, we demonstrate how an instancebased learning (IBL) cognitive model, implemented in a cognitive architecture (Adaptive Control of Thought–Rational), can be used to model an individual’s decisions in a cybersecurity defense task, accounting for both population average and individual variances. The same IBL model structure with identical architectural parameters generates the full range of human behavior through stochastic memory retrieval processes operating over and contributing to unique experiences. Recurrence quantification analyses allow us to look beyond average behavior between and within individuals to sequential patterns of trial-to-trial behavior. We show how model-tracing and knowledge-tracing techniques can be used to align the model to an individual in real time to drive adaptive and personalized signaling algorithms for a cybersecurity defense system. We also present a method for introspecting into the cognitive model to gain further insight into the cognitive salience of features factored into individual decisions. The combination of techniques provides a blueprint for personalized modeling of individuals. We discuss the results and implications of this adaptive and personalized method for cybersecurity defense and more generally for intelligent artifacts tailored to individual differences in domains such as human–machine teaming.

Keywords: Personalization; Individual differences; Model tracing; Cognitive salience; Instance-based learning; ACT-R; Cyber deception

Modeling individual differences in cognition is important for developing theories that explain the full range of human behavior as well as for using cognitive models to drive personalized, adaptive systems for human–machine interactions. As Estes (1956), Newell (1973), and Siegler (1987) have each pointed out long ago, if we account for only the average of human performance then we run the risk of overlooking or misinterpreting the true underlying processes that contribute to individual performance. Lee and Webb (2005) noted that many models of cognition are evaluated against data that have been averaged across individuals. The common solution to model individual differences is therefore to parameterize the model differently and separately for each participant or, as Lee and Webb suggested, to generate a family of different models that can be parameterized to model specific groups of participants. In this paper, we demonstrate that, when modeling human decision making from experience, a single cognitive model built according to instance-based learning theory (IBLT; Gonzalez, Lerch, & Lebiere, 2003) can account for both the average of human performance as well as the individual variance without the need for extensive parameterization. Thus, in combination with traditional model-tracing techniques (e.g., Anderson, Corbett, Koedinger, & Pelletier, 1995), instance-based learning (IBL) models can be used to tailor a system to an individual.

IBLT describes how decisions are made through learning and feedback from repeated, dynamic interactions with the environment (Gonzalez, 2013). According to IBLT, decisions are made by generalizing across past experiences. In a given context, experiences are encoded as instances or chunks in declarative memory that are represented by the contextual features in which the decision is made, the decision or action made, and the outcome of the decision. In new situations, a decision is made by generating an expected utility of each possible action from memory and selecting the action that maximizes that utility. The generation of expected utilities is made through a memory retrieval process called blending (Gonzalez et al. 2003; Lebiere, 1999) that aggregates across past instances based on their similarity to the current contextual features and the recency and frequency of the experience in memory. Because the activation quantities involved in memory retrieval include a random component, the expected utilities generated are themselves stochastic, making the decision probabilistic without the action selection process itself including a stochastic component.

IBLT has been used to model decision-making processes across several domains (Gonzalez, 2022; Hertwig, 2015). Some applications include repeated binary-choice decisions (Gonzalez & Dutt, 2011; Lebiere, Gonzalez, & Martin, 2007), multi-person/multi-choice games such as backgammon (Sanner, Anderson, Lebiere, & Lovett, 2000), rock-paper-scissors (West & Lebiere, 2001), and Stackelberg security games (SSGs; Abbasi et al., 2016), dynamic environments such as social dilemmas (Gonzalez, Ben-Asher, Martin, & Dutt, 2015; Juvina, Saleem, Martin, Gonzalez, & Lebiere, 2013; Lebiere, Wallach, & West, 2000), supply chain management (Gonzalez & Lebiere, 2005), resource allocation (Gonzalez et al., 2003), and automated detection systems (Thomson, Cranford, Somers, & Lebiere, 2024; Thomson, Lebiere, Bennati, Shakarian, & Nunes, 2015). These examples highlight the theory’s generalizability in modeling decisions from experience (Gonzalez, 2023).

Individual differences emerge from several different sources. When modeling decision making, individual differences may arise from differences in strategy (e.g., Bröder & Newell, 2008), or differences in algorithmic or architectural parameters that reflect cognitive mechanisms (e.g., working memory capacity; Lovett, Reder, & Lebiere, 1999), or differences in knowledge about the structure of the task or domain and experiential knowledge (see Rehling, Lovett, Lebiere, Reder, & Demiral, 2004). IBLT is a domain-general, memory-based theory of experiential learning that does not require explicit engineering of strategies, and thus resides in this last category. Individual differences are modeled through the effects of prior knowledge and experiential learning through feedback.

IBLT describes a general process for making decisions from experience and is grounded in memory retrieval mechanisms. When grounded in a cognitive architecture such as Adaptive Control of Thought–Rational (ACT-R; Anderson & Lebiere, 1998; Anderson et al., 2004), IBL models are behavior generative models that not only explain the statistics of the environment and the probability of making decisions in particular situations but also explain human cognition. Given an accurate representation of the process in which decisions are made in a particular context, IBL models require very little, if any, data to make accurate predictions of aggregate human behavior (see Cranford et al., 2020a). Individual differences in decision making are thus explained by stochasticity in memory retrieval processes and the unique sequence of experiences of an individual. IBL models can therefore reflect individual differences without the need for individual parameterization.

Modeling a specific individual, however, requires aligning the experiences of a model with that of an individual. For this reason, IBL models can combine naturally with model-tracing techniques, commonly used to adjust feedback provided to the student in intelligent tutoring systems (see Anderson et al., 1995). Model tracing can be used to align the model’s knowledge and experience with that of the human to make accurate predictions of their performance that can be used to adapt and personalize human–machine interactions. The alignment helps ensure that future model predictions are adapted and optimized to the human’s experience. For example, geometry tutors use model tracing to keep track of where errors are made so that the learning experience can be tailored to the individual (Anderson, Boyle, & Yost, 1986). By tracking an individual’s experience, model tracking can be used to synchronize an IBL model with the human’s observed actions and experience. After each decision, the instance saved to the model’s memory reflects the human’s decision and outcome rather than its own predictions. Therefore, future model predictions are based on the experience of the human and not the model’s own history of experience. As shown in Cranford et al. (2020a), with more experiences to draw from, IBL models make more accurate predictions of a particular human’s actions.

Understanding an individual’s experience is very important for personalizing models, but understanding how features are represented and weighed can provide unique insight into how an individual makes decisions. In addition to aligning the model’s knowledge and experience to an individual, another method that can be used to help explain an individual’s decision making is by examining the cognitive salience of features in an IBL model (Mitsopoulos et al., 2022; Somers, Mitsopoulos, Lebiere, & Thomson, 2019). This method introspects into the cognitive model to learn what features are most important for an individual’s decision making, which can further inform how to personalize the cognitive model and adapt a system.

Our approach for using IBLT to model an individual and personalize systems can be applied to a broad range of domains and tasks that involve dynamic decision making and experiential learning, including tutoring or training and explainable artificial intelligence for human– machine teaming (Mitsopoulos et al., 2022). To demonstrate the usefulness and practical value of our approach, we examine decision making in an abstraction of a cybersecurity defense task called the Insider Attack Game (IAG). In the IAG, an attacker chooses which of six targets to attack and is then sent a signal, which is sometimes deceptive, about whether the target is currently being monitored by a defender for which the attacker must decide to continue their attack or withdraw. The attacker makes repeated decisions, and the system predetermines which targets to defend and which targets to send signals for each trial. Therefore, this task offers a good example of how we can use cognitive models of an individual (here the attacker) to adapt a system to that individual (here the allocation of defenders and signals).

Modeling individual differences requires understanding how well the cognitive model can account for the wide range of individual variability as well as understanding how and why a specific individual’s decisions adapt over time. In order to evaluate the cognitive model’s ability to account for the range of individual differences in decision making, we use recurrence quantification analysis to examine individual patterns in sequential decision making (Marwan & Webber, 2015). Model introspection of the cognitive salience of features then provides an explanation for why individuals make their decisions. Combined, the methods presented in this paper provide an avenue toward better understanding inter- and intra-individual variability in decision making.

In this paper, we demonstrate using recurrence quantification analysis how an IBL cognitive model, implemented in the ACT-R cognitive architecture, accounts for both population average and individual variances and can be used to model an individual’s decisions in the IAG. We also describe how model-tracing and knowledge-tracing techniques can be used to adapt the model to account for individual behavior in real time. The combined methods are used to drive adaptive and personalized defense algorithms for the cybersecurity defense system. We present methods for introspecting into the cognitive model to gain a deeper understanding of an individual’s decision making (i.e., feature salience). Finally, we discuss how we can use this information to further personalize models and the broader implications of using IBL models for modeling individual differences in decision making from experience.

## 1. An IBL model of a cybersecurity defense task

## 1.1. The IAG

The IAG was designed as a two-stage SSG to investigate the influence of deceptive signals on cyber-attacker decision making in an insider attack scenario (Cranford, Gonzalez, et al., 2021). Players take the role of an insider attacker and make repeated decisions of “hacking” computers. In the first stage, attackers must decide which of six targets to attack as depicted in Fig. 1a. However, they must avoid the two analysts (defenders) that monitor one target each. An example target is shown in the zoomed inset of Fig. 1a. Attackers are presented with all information about the reward received if they successfully attack a target that is not monitored, the penalty received if they attack a target that is monitored, and the probability that the target is being monitored. After selecting a target, in the second stage, the attacker is presented with a message signaling whether the computer is being monitored (e.g., see Fig. 1b). The message is always truthful when claiming a target is not being monitored. However, the attacker is informed that the message is sometimes deceptive when claiming the target is being monitored. The attacker must decide to either continue the attack and earn the reward or penalty, depending on the true underlying coverage, or withdraw and earn zero points. Attackers are incentivized to earn as many points as possible across four rounds of 25 trials each; a new set of targets is presented each round.

The defense algorithm in the IAG, the strong Stackelberg equilibrium with persuasion (peSSE; Tambe, 2011; Xu, Rabinovich, Dughmi, & Tambe, 2015), was designed to optimize the rate at which deceptive messages are sent so that belief in the signal is maintained, under the assumption that adversaries make perfectly rational decisions. In the first stage, the algorithm optimizes the allocation of the two defenders based on the reward and penalty values of the targets so that the expected value of all targets is equal, and no target is more favorable than another. Defenders are assigned to targets across trials according to the derived probabilities (these are the monitoring probabilities attackers see). In the second stage, the algorithm optimizes the rate of deceptive signals. If signals were only truthful, the expected value would be negative when indicating that a target is being monitored. The peSSE determines the probability with which to send deceptive signals so that the expected value given a signal increases to zero, and under assumptions of perfect rationality, an adversary will defer to the safe option and withdraw. In the IAG, with a 1:3 defender-target ratio, the target is monitored, and the signal is present and truthful on 1/3rd of trials, on average. Therefore, the peSSE can send deceptive signals up to 1/2 of the trials when the target is not monitored before the expected value becomes greater than zero. Thus, the peSSE increases the perceived coverage of the system by finding the optimal combination of bluffing (sending a deceptive message that the target is monitored when it is not) and truth-telling (sending a truthful message that the target is covered) so that a rational attacker would always withdraw in the presence of a signal. In the IAG, the coverage and signaling of targets are predetermined across trials based on the peSSE and are the same for all participants.

## 1.2. The IBL model of human behavior in the IAG

The IBL model was created in the ACT-R cognitive architecture (Anderson & Lebiere, 1998; Anderson et al., 2004), which provides a theoretical framework that accurately simulates human-like cognition and processes such as memory retrieval, pattern matching, and decision making. For the IAG, the contextual features include the reward, penalty, monitoring probability, and signal. The decision/action is to attack or withdraw and the outcome/utility is the reward or penalty earned given the action and whether the target was monitored or not. For each decision, the IBL model uses ACT-R’s blending mechanism (Lebiere, 1999) to retrieve an expected outcome of attacking a target by interpolating across previously experienced outcomes. The expected outcome therefore reflects the contextual similarity of the present instance to previous instances weighted by their probability of retrieval and is computed with the following equation:

$$
V = \underset {V _ {t}} {\operatorname{argmin}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} P _ {i} \times \operatorname{Sim} (V _ {t}, v _ {i t}) ^ {2}.\tag{1}
$$

The value, V , is the interpolated value based on matching chunks i, weighted by their retrieval probability $P _ { i }$ . The similarity function, Sim $( V _ { t } , \nu _ { i t } ) ^ { 2 }$ , is used to compare the outcomes in memory chunks $\nu _ { i t }$ and candidate consensus values $V _ { t }$ and is effectively the error function to be minimized. In the simplest case, where the outcomes are numerical and the similarity function is linear, the process simplifies to a weighted average by the probability of retrieval.

The retrieval probability is derived from a Boltzmann function that is based on the activation strength of instances, which is influenced by power laws of frequency and recency, according to the ACT-R theory of memory retrieval (Anderson $\&$ Lebiere, 1998; Anderson et al., 2004), and the similarity or match between the current instance in memory and past instances:

$$
P _ {i} = \frac {e ^ {A i / t}}{\sum_ {j} e ^ {A _ {j} / t}},\tag{2}
$$

where $A _ { i }$ is the activation of an instance in memory, and t is the temperature, which is set to a neutral value of 1.0.

The activation $A _ { i }$ of a chunk i is determined by the following equation:

$$
A _ {i} = \ln \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} t _ {j} ^ {- d} + M P * \sum_ {k} \operatorname{Sim} \left(v _ {k}, c _ {k}\right) + \varepsilon_ {i}.\tag{3}
$$

Recency and frequency are reflected in the power law of practice and forgetting, represented by the first term, where $t _ { j }$ is the time since the jth occurrence of chunk i and d is the decay rate (set to the default ACT-R value of 0.5). The similarity between contextual features is reflected in a partial matching process, represented by the second term, where here $S i m ( \nu _ { k } , c _ { k } )$ is the similarity between the actual memory value and the current value for feature k and is scaled by the mismatch penalty (MP), which is set to 1.0. Similarities for numeric features are linearly scaled from 0.0 (an exact match) to −1.0, whereas symbolic values are either an exact match or maximally different, −2.5 (and is larger to ensure non-overlap between values of the signal: present and absent). The term $\varepsilon _ { i }$ represents transient noise, a random value from a logistic distribution with a mean of zero and variance parameter s of 0.25 (common ACT-R value; e.g., Lebiere, 1999), and introduces stochasticity in retrieval.

The IBL model played the same game as humans in purely generative fashion. In the first stage of the IAG, the features of the decision include the monitoring probability [0.0, 1.0], the reward [1, 10], and the penalty [−1, −10]. The model generates an expected outcome for each target, via blending across previous outcomes, and selects the target with the highest expected outcome. In the second stage, the only feature in the decision is the signal [present, absent] and the model generates a new expected outcome of attacking. A straightforward decision rule is then applied: if the value is greater than zero the model attacks, else it withdraws, and ground truth feedback is given.

The model saves two instances to memory on each trial. One represents the expectation generated during the decision to continue the attack or withdraw (includes the features: signal, action, and expected outcome), and the other represents the ground truth decision and feedback received (includes all features: signal, reward, penalty, monitoring probability, action, and ground truth outcome). Thus, both instances influence future attack decisions but only the latter influences future selection decisions. Storing the expectations as well as the ground

## 1.3. Assessing individual differences in the IAG from human and IBL model results

Cranford, Gonzalez, et al. (2021) compared the performance of 98 humans to that of 1000 IBL model agents. The design choices and parameter settings described above were found to best describe the full range of human data. However, each IBL model agent performs differently due to stochasticity in memory retrieval operating over, and contributing to, unique experiences stored in memory. Thus, the same IBL model structure can represent a population of human attackers without the need to individually modify each agent’s architectural (i.e., meta) parameters such as learning rate, activation noise, or decay rate. The left panel of Fig. 2 shows the mean probability of attack across trials for the humans, compared to the model. The model is highly accurate at predicting human performance (total root mean squared error $[ \mathrm { R M S E } ] = 0 . 0 4 )$ , even matching the trial-to-trial variations that reflect the underlying coverage and signaling schedules (total $r = . 7 3 )$ , and that accuracy increases across blocks. Additionally, the right panel of Fig. 2 shows that the model accurately reflects the individual variance in overall attack probabilities. The distribution shows that, like humans, some model agents attack at a low rate, while a large proportion attack at a rate greater than 95%.

To further show how the cognitive model accounts for individual differences in the IAG, we examined the patterns of choices (attack/withdraw) using recurrence plots and recurrence quantification analyses (McCormick, Blaha, & Gonzalez, 2020; Marwan & Webber, 2015). Recurrence analysis was designed for the analysis of nonlinear dynamics of complex systems and is used to examine the repetition of states in dynamic systems. From its origins in physics, recurrence analysis has been applied to quantify temporal patterns in electroencephalogram signals (Marwan & Webber, 2015), discourse comprehension (for reviews, see Coco & Dale, 2014; Wallot, 2017), and more recently, decision making (McCormick, Blaha, & Gonzalez,

2020). Recurrence analysis can be viewed as a discrete form of Granger causality analysis (Granger, 1969) applied to the same series. In dynamical decision-making tasks, analyses that aggregate over decisions can obscure or even conceal individual learning and adaptation over time. Recurrence plots can help visualize individual differences in recurrent patterns of decision sequences. Such analysis can help researchers better understand how recency and frequency of past experiences influence future decisions, how individuals learn and adapt over time, and the range of individual differences for these metrics.

Recurrence plots are used to visualize the repetition of states in dynamic systems over time. The x- and y- axes of the plots represent time points (e.g., trials in a laboratory decisionmaking task) where the bottom left origin represents the first time point on both the x- and y axes and increases at the same intervals to the right and up, respectively. Each coordinate is then assigned a color based on the recurrence of states, also known as recurrence points. For example, for states $S ^ { 1 , \ldots , n }$ at trials $x , y = 1 , \ldots , T , \mathrm { i f } \; S _ { x } ^ { j } = S _ { y } ^ { j }$ then that cell will be filled with color j, but if $S _ { x } ^ { j } e S _ { y } ^ { j }$ , then the cell will be white (or not colored). However, the main diagonal that compares the same trials (i.e., when trial $x = y )$ is referred to as the line of incidence, and these cells are also white because these points are excluded from the analysis.

Figs. 3 and 4 show recurrence plots for humans and the model, respectively. For the model, we randomly selected 100 model agents to generate an array of plots similar in number to that of the humans, which were representative of the full sample. Each plot in the grid represents an individual participant/agent. The plots are sorted by the overall mean probability of attack where the top left plot is the agent with the lowest probability of attack, and the bottom right is the agent with the largest probability of attack. The x- and y-axes of each recurrence plot are trials in the game, with the bottom left origin being trial one. For our task, each type of decision is a state. Dark green points indicate the recurrence of attack decisions, and light green points indicate the recurrence of withdraw decisions. Meanwhile, white points indicate switching between decisions or no recurrence (excluding the line of incidence). For example, if an agent attacks on both trials one and two, then the cell at coordinate (1, 2)—and coordinate (2,1) since the plots are symmetrical across the line of incidence—will be colored dark green. If they withdraw on both trials one and two, then the cell will be colored light green. However, if they attack on trial one but withdraw on trial two, then the cell will be colored white.

The plots can be visually examined to understand the pattern of decisions across trials. The horizontal and vertical bars can be examined to identify when the same decision was made at other trials in the game. Vertical bars show the recurrence of a decision at trial x to other trials in the game, while horizontal bars show the recurrence of a decision at trial y, compared to other trials in the game. For example, if an agent attacks on trial two and on trials 10–15, then there will be a vertical bar of dark green at coordinates (2, 10–15) and a horizontal bar at coordinates (10–15, 2). Large vertical or horizontal structures are indicative of laminar states in which agents make the same decision over extended periods of time and provide information about the stability of an agent’s decisions.

Meanwhile, diagonals that run parallel to the line of incidence can be examined to identify repetitions of sequential patterns of behavior. For example, dark green diagonals mean agents made a similar sequence of attack decisions earlier in the game, light green diagonals mean agents made a similar sequence of withdraw decisions, while white diagonals (again, excluding the line of incidence) mean agents were more random and did not repeat the same patterns of decision making. Large, non-white diagonal patterns could indicate repetitions of the same decision or repetitions of matching sequences (e.g., switching between decisions every nth trial). For example, if an agent attacks three times and then withdraws twice and has made this same decision sequence earlier in the game, then there will be a diagonal of three dark green squares and two light green squares. The diagonal structures are indicative of deterministic states and provide information about the stochasticity or predictability of an agent’s decisions. These structures are thus important for examining sequential decision-making behavior (e.g., strategies such as win-stay-lose-shift, hot-stove, stickiness, and recency).

The recurrence plots in both Figs. 3 and 4 show that a large group of agents attack almost all the time, indicated by large swaths of dark green, but also that a large subset of agents display substantial individual differences in decision patterns. Some agents shift from mostly withdrawing behavior early on before attacking more often on later trials (i.e., mostly light green cells towards the bottom left of the plot and mostly dark green toward the top right of the plot). Other agents mostly attack early on before withdrawing more often (i.e., mostly dark green toward the bottom left and light green toward the top right). Still some agents tend to switch more evenly between attacking and withdrawing throughout the game (i.e., the plaid patterns that include more white stripes and fewer large patches of the same color). And finally, some agents tend to withdraw most often across trials (i.e., large swaths of light green). Importantly, a visual comparison of the recurrence plots indicates that the IBL model displays a similar range of individual differences and effectively produces similar classes of decision makers as seen in the human data. The same initial model produces a range of behaviors through a combination of differences in simulated practice trials and stochasticity in retrieval, which produce different trajectories of experience.

Recurrence quantification analyses can be performed to quantitatively examine individual differences in patterns of decision making and to compare a model’s performance to that of humans. Fig. 5 plots a suite of recurrence quantification analyses to highlight the similarity between distributions (as kernel density estimates) of recurrence patterns for humans, compared to the IBL model. We examined a suite of measures formulated in Marwan and Webber (2015) using the R crqa library (Coco & Dale, 2014). The first measure is the recurrence rate, which examines the overall proportion of recurrent points in the plots (i.e., percent of colored squares). This measure can be used to estimate how often the same decisions are made across trials. The results reveal a similar bimodal distribution for both the model and humans. A large proportion of agents have a recurrence rate of just over 50% and another large proportion have very high recurrence rates near or at 100%. The former group switches decisions more often indicating either randomness or greater deliberation, while the latter group is indicative of agents that very often or always make the same decision (i.e., most agents always attack, but a few almost always withdraw).

The next six measures examine the diagonals for repetitions in sequential patterns of decisions. Determinism measures the percent of recurrence points that form diagonal lines. Higher values indicate more sequential patterns of decisions such as making the same decision across consecutive trials, or consistently making the same pattern of decisions across the game. Lower values indicate more randomness in decisions. The results reveal a similar bimodal distribution for humans and the model in which a large proportion have very high determinism, which can be explained by the very high attack rate in the game. Meanwhile, another smaller group have a lower, but still relatively high determinism, indicative of mostly steady patterns with occasional unpredictable transitions.

The number of diagonal lines straightforwardly measures the number of diagonal lines with a minimum length of two, while average and maximum (abbreviated Max.) diagonal length are measures of the average and maximum length of diagonals, respectively. These results reveal that, compared to humans, more of the model agents have more diagonals of shorter length. Model agents have a greater tendency for their consistent patterns of behavior to be interrupted, which could be attributed to stochasticity in the retrieval mechanism.

Fig. 5. Recurrence quantification analysis distributions for humans, compared to the IBL model.

Finally, Shannon entropy measures the complexity of the diagonal line lengths, where higher values indicate greater variance in the distribution and thus greater complexity. Meanwhile, normalized entropy is the Shannon entropy normalized by the number of diagonal lines observed in the recurrence plot. The model reveals a greater proportion of agents with lower complexity likely because the length and thus range of diagonal lengths is typically smaller than for humans. However, when normalized by the number of diagonals, the complexity for both humans and the model is very similar and roughly follows a normal distribution except for a small group of agents that display greater complexity and represents those agents that switch decisions more often.

The final two measures examine the vertical structures for repetitions of the same decisions. Laminarity measures the percent of recurrence points that form vertical lines, which represents the frequency of sequences where decisions remain stable. Like for determinism, the large group of agents that have very high laminarity represents the overall high attack rate and those agents that consistently make the same decision. Meanwhile, as for humans, some agents’ decisions are less stable. Finally, trapping time measures the average length of the vertical lines, which indicates the average time the same decision is made before switching. Compared to humans, a larger proportion of model agents have lower trapping time, and thus switch decisions faster. This measure complements the analyses of diagonal line numbers and length and can also be attributed to stochasticity in the retrieval mechanisms resulting in occasional exploration and escaping from a laminar state.

Across all measures, the IBL model displays very similar shapes of distributions as those of humans. Such similarity would not be achieved by simply feeding randomized or normalized data through the analysis because the result would be normal distributions, whereas the current results revealed many bimodal distributions. The overall pattern of results suggests the model is very good at representing the full range of recurrence patterns seen in the human population. These results highlight the role of human experiential learning and adaptation in the IAG, and the ability of the cognitive model to reproduce the online learning and decisionmaking capabilities of humans.

Recurrence plots provide unique insight into how well the model matches individual vari ances in learning and adaptation over time. While distributions such as kernel density estima tions are useful for showing how well the model represents the full range of human performance, recurrence quantification values for individual recurrence plots can be used to identify unique patterns of behavior across agents and/or categorize agents into classes of decision makers. For example, cluster analyses could be used to identify the range of patterns of behaviors that humans exhibit, and comparisons to the model can be made to determine whether the model accurately captures the full range of behavior or even to predict additional patterns of behavior not represented by the human sample. Recurrence plots and recurrence quantification analyses can thus be valuable tools for examining individual differences for dynamic decision-making tasks.

## 2. Applying individualized models for adaptive, personalized systems

Modeling the range of individual differences in the population is informative, but modeling a specific individual requires greater precision. The IBL model shows that individuals learn from and adapt their behavior through repeated interactions in the IAG. Therefore, a signaling scheme that adapts to an individual’s experience should fare better than a static scheme. Since the IBL model can accurately predict both the average and individual variance of human decision making in the IAG, it could effectively be used to drive adaptive, personalized solutions for deceptive signaling. However, while the recurrence plots show how the IBL model can account for individual differences in attack decisions, the model is purely generative, and personalized systems must be able to model a specific individual at a specific time. Therefore, we must align the IBL model with a specific individual by either selecting the model that best matches the human after each decision or by adapting the model in real time so that the model’s experiences align with that of the human.

Cranford et al. (2020a, 2020b) and Lebiere et al. (2023) present solutions for adaptive, personalized signaling in the IAG. The solutions combine the IBL model, which relies on individual history of experiences, with model- and knowledge-tracing techniques to track an individual’s decisions and make predictions of their behavior as they interact with the IAG. These predictions can then be used to inform the system on how to adjust the rate of deceptive signals to maintain the individual’s belief in the signal. For example, if an individual’s belief in the signal wanes, eliminating deceptive signals for a short period of time can help restore belief in the signal.

Model tracing and knowledge tracing are techniques commonly used in intelligent tutoring systems (see Anderson et al., 1995) to align a model’s history of experience with that of a specific human. As the model performs the task alongside the human, instances are modified to reflect the decisions and outcome of the human. The alignment ensures that future model predictions are optimized to the interaction with that individual. With more trials, the model is expected to make more accurate predictions of a particular human’s actions, as the model’s memory continues to align with that of the human. Cranford et al. (2020a) and Lebiere et al. (2023) show that the probability of agreement between the model’s and the human’s decisions it traced continues to increase over time, and the overall mean probability of attack is highly correlated across participants, $r ^ { 2 } = . 9 5$

Cranford et al. (2020b) showed that, compared to the peSSE, a personalized cognitive signaling scheme was effective at reducing the probability of attack against a portion of participants, and the model accurately predicted this behavior a priori. However, there was a large portion of participants that continued to attack almost all the time despite being pre-dominantly presented with truthful signals throughout the game. The results of a follow-up survey revealed that many of these participants reported not paying attention to the signal when deciding whether to continue the attack or withdraw. Given the structure of the game, if one ignores the signal, the expected value of attacking is positive, so their behavior was not irrational given their feature representation of the decision. In fact, a version of the IBL model that does not consider the signal when generating an expected outcome of attacking the selected target attacked at a similar rate as these aggressive participants.

These results stress the importance of understanding the features that individuals consider in their decisions since one’s representation of the decision context strongly influences the chosen action. Therefore, to improve the personalized cognitive signaling scheme, we need to find additional ways to adapt the model to an individual. For the IAG, this may entail understanding the target selection preferences of an individual to anticipate their attack and shift coverage or adapting the representation of information to emphasize the relative importance of contextual features that contribute to an individual’s decisions. Toward these ends, we turn to a method of introspecting IBL models to determine the cognitive salience of features in decision making.

## 2.1. Introspecting IBL models through cognitive salience analyses

Feature representation plays an important role in human decisions, and while much is known about how experiences shape decisions through IBLT (e.g., frequency, recency, and similarity effects), and the underlying mechanisms, much more needs to be understood about what features are represented in the instances and how those features weigh in the decision. We could gain further insight about how to adapt a model to an individual if we understood what features they find salient or important. One possibility would be to model the process by which individuals select features to use in decisions (e.g., Martin, Lebiere, Fields, & Lennon, 2018). Modeling this process would bring additional insights into the cognitive biases introduced by switching between representations that include different sets of features (Lebiere, Blaha, Fallon, & Jefferson, 2021). Here, we instead use an approach analogous to the analytical introspection of chunk activations in the cognitive model described above regarding adaptive signaling. We consider the salient feature of a decision to be the feature that most influenced that decision, and the greater degree of salience a feature has, the more influential it was in the decision.

We term our approach cognitive salience in contrast to the gradient-based saliency of pixels used in image classification (e.g., Grün, Rupprecht, Navab, & Tombari, 2016). We use the term cognitive for two reasons. First, our approach calculates salience by introspecting into the cognitive mechanism of memory retrieval (i.e., blending). Second, the features of a cognitive model are typically of a higher level of abstraction than pixels, usually conceptual terms, which is typical of a cognitive-level description. Cognitive salience was first applied in an explainable artificial intelligence context (Mitsopoulos et al., 2022; Somers et al., 2019), where ACT-R was used to model a reinforcement learning-based agent.

We calculate salience by taking the derivative of the blending equation with respect to each feature:

$$
S \left(V _ {t}, f _ {k}\right) = \frac {M P}{t} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} P _ {i} \cdot \left(\frac {\partial \operatorname{Sim} \left(f _ {k} , v _ {i k}\right)}{\partial f _ {k}} - \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} P _ {j} \frac {\partial \operatorname{Sim} \left(f _ {k} , v _ {j k}\right)}{\partial f _ {k}}\right) \cdot v _ {i t}.\tag{3}
$$

This derivative gives us the degree of influence a particular feature $( f _ { k } )$ had in a decision $( V _ { t } )$ by quantifying the degree of change of the decision as a function of the change in the feature, where the degree of change reflects the similarity function used for the respective quantities. The value $S$ can be infinitely positive or negative. While the sign (±) of the value provides information about the direction of the impact of the feature (e.g., for larger positive values of the feature, positive salience results in higher expected outcomes from blending, and negative salience results in lower expected outcomes, and vice versa for negative values), the magnitude tells us which feature has the greater impact on the decision when comparing between features. Therefore, in all analyses below, we examine the absolute values of S.

We examined the salience of features during the first-stage selection decision and during the second-stage attack decision of the IBL model playing the IAG against the peSSE. During target selection, a perfectly rational attacker would display no preference for features because all targets have the same expected value. No one feature is more informative than another and does not differentiate targets since reward and penalty are determined independently and monitoring probability is set according to the distribution of those two variables according to the game theory algorithm. However, it is possible that, for boundedly rational humans who derive expected outcomes from very limited experiences, selection preferences could emerge if one feature becomes more salient than another.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 6. Cognitive salience analyses of the first-stage selection decision.

Note. The left panel shows the mean relative salience of each feature for each agent. The right panel shows the distribution of target selection preferences for each group of agents, defined by the agent’s most salient feature. Mprob = monitoring probability.

During the second-stage attack decision, individuals vary considerably in the probability of attack as shown in Figs. 2–4. It is therefore hypothesized that, when the signal is present, salience for the signal is lower for those participants with high probabilities of attack. The reasoning is that a lower salience for the signal means decisions are weighted more equally between signal types. When a signal is present, the blended expected outcome generated will be higher because more weight is given to instances where a signal is not present, which includes more positive outcomes. In contrast, higher salience would mean blended outcomes are more heavily weighted toward the current type of signal, and if a signal is present, then blending will give more weight to instances where a signal is present, which include more negative outcomes.

## 2.1.1. Cognitive salience analysis of the first-stage decision: Selection

Fig. 6 shows the results of the salience analysis of the first-stage selection decision. The saliences are calculated during the outcome generation process. When generating expected outcomes, the model interpolates from previous experiences, weighing those experiences by their similarity to the features of the current target (i.e., the reward, penalty, and monitoring probability). The left-panel plot examines the individual differences between model agents regarding the mean relative magnitude of the saliences. For each feature, we compute the average salience across trials for each individual and take their magnitude or absolute values.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 7. Cognitive salience analyses for second-stage attack decision.

Note. The left panel shows the mean salience across rounds for each player type. The right panel shows the mean expected outcome (i.e., blending value) for each player type. Solid lines indicate salience when a signal is absent, and dashed lines indicate salience when a signal is present.

Each point in this ternary plot represents the ratio of mean magnitude saliencies of the three features for each agent. The plot thus shows the relative importance of each feature for each individual. The results show that agents do not display any clear preference for features, on average, centering mostly around the middle point of the plot, indicating saliences for features are all close to the same magnitude. However, all agents display a higher salience for one of the features, even if the relative difference is miniscule, as indicated by the color coding. Some agents even extend toward the corners of the ternary plot, if only by a small percentage. Agents were therefore split into three groups depending on the feature that is overall most salient, the reward, penalty, or monitoring probability, to examine if these groups display any target selection preferences.

The right panel of Fig. 6 shows a scatterplot of target selections by the reward and penalty values of the selected target. The size of the dots indicates the percent of selections for that target within a round. Thus, the dominant color for a point indicates a greater percent of selections for that group on that target. The distributions of penalties and rewards for each “Max Saliency” group are shown as marginal plots on the right and top, respectively. The results reveal clear differences in target selection behavior between groups. The agents that have higher salience for the penalty tend to select the targets with bigger penalties but also the potential for greater rewards or lower monitoring probability. Note that in this case, the salience is negative, with more negative penalties leading to a higher probability of selection. Meanwhile, agents that have higher salience for reward tend to select the targets with bigger rewards but more moderate penalties. Finally, agents that have higher salience for monitoring probability tend to select the targets with smaller rewards and penalties and thus have lower monitoring probabilities. Preferences emerge through individual experience regarding what choices may result in potentially better rewards and are reflected in the cognitive salience metrics.

## 2.1.2. Cognitive salience analysis of the second-stage decision: Attack

Fig. 7 shows the results of the salience analysis of the second-stage attack decision. In the second-stage decision, it was hypothesized that aggressive attackers (i.e., those that attacked ≥95% of the time) may weigh the signal differently than the other, more cautious attackers. The left panel of Fig. 7 shows the mean magnitude saliencies for the signal feature across the four rounds. The breaks in the solid line for the signal-absent condition are trials in which every target was scheduled to present a signal. When the signal is absent, the salience for the signal is about equal in Round 1 but is higher for the aggressive attackers through the remainder of the game. For both player types, the salience is overall higher when the signal is absent than when the signal is present. When the signal is present, however, the salience of the signal is lower for aggressive attackers than for cautious ones. As predicted, when present, the signal is less influential in aggressive attackers’ decisions than in cautious attackers’ decisions.

The right panel of Fig. 7 shows the mean expected outcome for the attack decision across the four rounds. An interesting interaction presents itself when compared to the pattern for saliences. For expected outcomes, when the signal is absent, the aggressive attackers generate higher values than cautious attackers, echoing the pattern for saliences. However, in contrast to saliences, when the signal is present, cautious attackers generate lower expected outcomes than aggressive attackers.

These results suggest that salience reflects the influence that features have on memory retrieval when making decisions. A higher salience for a signal means that, for blending, more weight is given to past instances that have the same value as the current signal, and when salience is low for the signal, more weight is given to past instances that have a different value as the current signal so that probabilities are more evenly distributed across past instances. In this case, salience can be interpreted as an attentional weight given to the presence of a signal. When a signal is absent, the higher salience for aggressive attackers means more weight is given to past instances whose signal is absent. Because these instances have only positive values, the expected outcomes are inflated. When a signal is present, the lower salience for aggressive attackers means the probability of retrieving past instances whose signal is absent is higher, and more evenly distributed across all targets (hence the expected outcome by Round 4 is approximately equal to the true expected value, irrespective of the signal, of 1.43), and again the expected outcomes are inflated. Meanwhile, cautious attackers that have higher salience for the signal when present have expected outcomes near zero, which is the true expected value given a signal.

## 2.2. Implications of cognitive salience analysis for personalized IBL models

The cognitive salience results reveal important information about how individuals weigh features when making decisions from experience. The selection decision results revealed variations in preferences for targets based on the most salient feature even though all targets are of equal expected value. While the relative importance for a single feature was not strong for any individual, the salience values relate directly to individual actions and were informative measures of decision preferences. Meanwhile, the attack decision results revealed that the degree of salience for the signal has a direct impact on the probability of retrieving past instances, which in turn impacts the expected outcomes generated. The results provide unique insights into how individual differences can emerge through unique experiences. Understanding how an individual weighs the features in their decisions provides valuable evidence about how information is processed and how it impacts decisions, which is important for systems that rely on adaptive and personalized interventions.

The personalized cognitive signaling scheme from Cranford et al. (2020b) showed that aggressive attackers tended to report that they ignored the signal feature, and a model that omitted that feature from the representation was a better predictor of these aggressive attackers. Cognitive salience can inform what features are important in a decision, which could be used to adapt the model to better characterize the underlying representation of the decision. A more accurate model of an individual can provide more accurate predictions about their behavior, which can be used to improve automated systems. Additionally, cognitive salience information could be used to directly inform an adaptive system. For example, in the present cybersecurity task, the feature salience of the selection decision could be used to directly adapt the coverage of targets to more effectively defend against those individuals who ignore the signal during the attack decision. Examining cognitive salience with cognitive models provides valuable information about individual differences, and future research aims at exploring its utility for designing more effective personalized, adaptive signaling schemes for cyber defense.

## 3. Conclusion

In this paper, we have highlighted the suitability of IBLT for modeling individual differences when making decisions from experience. IBLT describes a generalized decisionmaking process and can explain individual choice variability through their unique experiences, accounting for memory phenomena such as recency, frequency, and similarity, without the need for individual parameterization. IBL models are therefore useful for personalizing and adapting systems to an individual by tracking their history of interactions in a dynamic environment.

Recurrence quantification analyses proved to be a useful method for examining individual patterns in sequential decision making. The suite of metrics provides a diagnostic tool for evaluating the cognitive model’s ability to account for the range of individual differences in decision making. Through recurrence quantification analysis, we showed that our IBL model was able to account for the variability of the population, and model- and knowledge-tracing techniques allowed us to adapt the model to specific individuals.

Combining IBL models with model- and knowledge-tracing techniques provides an efficient method to personalize human–machine interactions. IBL models require very little data regarding an individual’s experiences to make accurate predictions of that individual’s future behavior. IBL models can be applied quite efficiently, requiring very few production rules or other engineering effort or complexity, and can account for individual learning by modifying declarative memory chunks to match that of the individual being modeled. When grounded in a cognitive architecture such as ACT-R, IBL models provide constrained mechanisms to personalize decisions, offering not only decision predictions but also explanations of behavior. Methods of introspection into the cognitive model, such as cognitive salience, may prove to be practically useful in further tailoring IBL models to an individual to better inform adaptive, personalized systems.

Current and future research is aimed at applying these methods to other domains. For example, we have designed an IBL model that explains human susceptibility to phishing emails (see Cranford, Singh, Aggarwal, Lebiere, & Gonzalez, 2021) and are developing methods that use the model to drive personalized anti-phishing training. In other lines of research, we are exploring ways to incorporate cognitive salience metrics into the personalized cognitive signaling algorithm. One important goal for this research is to be able to use the fully fledged IBL model with model-tracing techniques. Therefore, it is imperative that we address scalability issues. As the number of experiences increases, the computation time for the blending mechanism increases linearly. An IBL model may become nonviable after a long period of model tracing or if the model is initialized with a large database of knowledge. Therefore, future research is aimed at exploring methods that are scalable for real-world deployment. One method is using only the architectural mechanisms necessary for modeling purposes as enabled by ACT-UP (Reitter & Lebiere, 2010), an alternative toolkit implementation of ACT-R that allows computational tractability by abstracting and isolating cognitive mechanisms to leverage only those needed. Similarly, CogIBL (Mitsopoulos et al., 2022) uses memory retrieval and blending mechanisms to model utility-based learning in a machine learning framework to leverage equation vectorization and parallel processing. Vectorization of an IBL model’s memory is a method that could greatly increase computational speed (e.g., Kelly, Arora, West, & Reitter, 2020). Additionally, methods for selecting only a representative subset of memories instead of using the entire memory for blending could help limit computational costs. Future applications of personalized IBL models will greatly benefit from scalable solutions that afford introspection yet retain their explainability and predictability.
